theme: In my distress I called; I lift my eyes to the hills
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 120 and Psalm 121. These are the first two Songs of Ascents, which pilgrims sang on the way up to Jerusalem. Psalm 120 starts in distress far from home, and Psalm 121 lifts its eyes to the hills.
settingTheScene: Psalms 120 to 134 are the Songs of Ascents, sung by pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem for the festivals. After the exile, they may also have been the songs of those returning. Psalm 120 begins in a foreign place: “Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace.” Psalm 121 is the voice of someone on the journey who asks where help comes from. They belong at this point in the plan as songs for exiles on the road home.
observation: “In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me” (120:1).
“Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue” (120:2).
“Woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!” (120:5).
“Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war” (120:6-7).
“I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?” (121:1).
“My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (121:2).
“He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber” (121:3).
“The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore” (121:8).
interpretation:
Psalm 120 begins with a testimony and then a prayer. “In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me.” The psalmist remembers a time of rescue, and in the present he again needs it. His troubles are liars. Deceitful tongues surround him. He asks God to deal with them as arrows and burning coals. He is in a foreign place, Meshech and Kedar, far-off lands, a symbolic way of saying that he is among people who do not share his values. His last line is poignant: “I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.” It is the lament of anyone who longs for peace and meets hostility.

Psalm 121 is the answer. The pilgrim looks up at the hills of Judea. Some read the question as fear: the hills held pagan shrines and bandits. Others read it as longing for Zion. Either way, the answer is clear: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.” The one who made the hills is greater than they are. Help does not come from the landscape, but from its Creator.

Then the psalm uses a word again and again: keep. The LORD is your keeper. He will not let your foot slip. He does not sleep. He is your shade at your right hand. The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. He will keep your life. He will keep your going out and your coming in.

Together the two psalms give the journey of faith: from the foreign land of distress to the God who keeps. The travelers learn that their security does not depend on the road but on the one who walks it with them.
connection: Jesus said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5, paraphrasing Deuteronomy 31:6), and “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). John 10:28 says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand. Jude 24 says he is able to keep you from stumbling. 1 Peter 1:5 says we are guarded by God’s power. Psalm 127 and Mark 4:38 remind us that Jesus slept in the boat, but the Father does not slumber. Romans 12:18 says, “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.”
application:
When you are in distress, begin as Psalm 120 does: remember a past time that God answered you.

Pray Psalm 121 as a blessing over someone who is traveling or starting a new job.

When you feel surrounded by hostility, say aloud, “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.”
prayerPrompts: Tell God what distresses you and ask him to answer.
Lift your eyes to him as your help.
Thank him that he will keep you.
